world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Tem (temm1241) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Tchagbalé 2001 'L'accent tonal du Tem' (TAPS 2001 proceedings), was located in full text: the original Bielefeld TAPS site is dead with no archived copy at the Internet Archive, but the whole proceedings are mirrored under Dafydd Gibbon's homepage (wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/gibbon/Dafydd_Gibbon_Publication_PDFs/TAPS/), and the 17-page PDF plus the abstract HTML were downloaded, and. It is squarely about accent placement in Tem and is first-hand by the language's principal describer: Tem has one tonal accent per word, realised as H (L = unaccented), morphologically supplied by the final suffix or grammatical markers, fixed on that suffix or floating one syllable left (final or penultimate in nouns and infinitives), free rather than fixed-position, no dynamic stress; conclusion 'Le Tem est donc une langue à accent tonal'. Already-on-disk sources read for context agree: Tchagbalé 1984 (JWAL 14(1): 30) says each phonological word bears at most one H tone and suspects it is an accent; Müller 1905 §5 (p. 253) reports an impressionistic dynamic accent within the last three syllables that shifts with plural suffixes, plus H/L tone; De Craene 1986 (SAL 17(1)) describes a two-tone H/L system with H-spread and downstep and is silent on accent. Nothing relevant remains unacquired from the item list; Tchagbalé's 1976 thesis and 1998 thèse d'État remain unlocated online (prior check), but the 2001 paper explicitly supersedes the 1976 tone-language analysis and is the best available deciding statement for a new catalog record (coding suggestion: tonal accent, culminative, final/penultimate, morphologically conditioned; not stress). all discovery was done with direct download and automated download.

new_statements.quote: § 5. 2. Akzent. Der dynamische Akzent eines Wortes scheint mir über die drittletzte Silbe, auf welcher er selten ruht, nicht hinauszugehen. Bei der Anfügung der Pluralsuffixe erleidet er vielfach eine Verschiebung. — Neben dem dynamischen scheint auch ein Tonakzent vorhanden, ein Tiefton = ` und ein Hochton = ´.
new_statements.translation: §5. 2. Accent. The dynamic accent of a word seems to me not to go back beyond the third-from-last syllable, on which it seldom rests. When the plural suffixes are added it frequently undergoes a shift. — Beside the dynamic accent a tonal accent also seems to be present, a low tone = ` and a high tone = ´.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: (36 pp., text layer present). Rendered p. 3 of the extract (printed p. 253, running head 'Müller: Beitrag zur Kenntnis der Tem-Sprache (Nord-Togo). 253') at 150 dpi and read the page image: '§ 5. 2. Akzent. Bei der Anfügung der Pluralsuffixe erleidet er vielfach eine Verschiebung. — Neben dem dynamischen scheint auch ein Tonakzent vorhanden, ein Tiefton = ` und ein Hochton = ´.' -- verbatim as quoted (spaced-letter emphasis on 'dynamische Akzent' and 'Tonakzent' in the original; line-break hyphen 'dritt-letzte' rejoined). Surrounding context: §4 consonant p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Müller (impressionistic, hedged 'scheint mir'): intensity stress falls inside a final three-syllable window and rarely on the antepenult, i.e. normally on the penult or the final syllable (he does not decide between them), and it moves when plural class suffixes are added; separately there is a high/low tonal opposition. Modern first-hand descriptions (Tchagbalé 1984; De Craene 1986; Peace Corps 2010) describe Tem as a two-tone (H vs L/unmarked) language and give no stress rule; Tchagbalé 1984 adds that a phonological word carries at most one H, imposed 'à un endroit quelconque du mot phonique' by the lexeme, and that this 'ton haut' may really be an accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source read.
new_statements.exceptions: Müller: stress shifts under plural suffixation; verb paradigms show '(Ton-)Akzent' alternations by aspect and person (§57-60), e.g. final-syllable 'Betonung' in durative stems. Tchagbalé 1984: words built on a -th lexeme are entirely low (no H at all); certain derivatives (diminutive /yɩ/, agentive /dʊ/) demand to carry the word's single H.
new_statements.domain_note: Müller speaks of the word ('eines Wortes'), citation forms from Sokodé-area speakers c. 1900. Tchagbalé's culminativity domain is the 'mot phonique' (lexeme + derivatives + class suffix, realised without virtual pause). De Craene's tone rules (H-spread onto following L, downstep) apply within the clause.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Tem/Kotokoli proper (temm1241, iso kdh) as spoken around Sokodé (Tchaoudjo), central Togo: Müller 1905 'Tem/Tim (Temba, Kotokoli, Tšaučo)', De Craene (SIL, Sokodé), Tchagbalé (native speaker). No dialect split is made for prosody; Müller notes Tem ~ Tim as a mere dialectal pronunciation difference.

new_statements.quote: Le Tem n'est donc pas une langue à tons mais une langue à accent. L'accent en question n'est pas un accent fixe n'intervenant qu'à la même position quelle que soit l'unité accentuelle; c'est un accent libre. [...] L'accent tem est donc un accent tonal. Il est (pour ce qui est du nom et de l'infinitif) associé au suffixe sur lequel il se fixe ou flotte à sa gauche. [...] Aussi doit-on s'attendre à un accent par mot, fixé sur la dernière ou l'avant-dernière syllabe. C'est le cas pour tout infinitif ; pour les noms, une minorité à plus de deux syllabes, peut comporter des schèmes tonals [...]
new_statements.translation: Tem is therefore not a tone language but an accent language. The accent in question is not a fixed accent occurring at the same position whatever the accentual unit; it is a free accent. [...] The Tem accent is therefore a tonal accent. It is (for nouns and infinitives) associated with the suffix, on which it is fixed or to whose left it floats. [...] So one should expect one accent per word, fixed on the last or the second-to-last syllable. That is the case for every infinitive; for nouns, a minority of more than two syllables may show tonal patterns [...]
new_statements.citation: Tchagbalé, Zakari (2001). L'accent tonal du Tem. In U. Gut, E. E. Urua & D. Gibbon (eds.), Proceedings of TAPS: Typology of African Prosodic Systems Workshop, Bielefeld University, 18-20 May 2001 (Bielefeld Occasional Papers in Typology 1), web edition, 17 pp.
new_statements.locator: PDF p. 7 (end of §2.1 'Construction du schème de base' and opening of §2.2 'Les schèmes inattendus dans les noms'); conclusion restated §4, PDF p. 16: 'Le Tem est donc une langue à accent tonal.'
new_statements.reading: Tem is a tonal-accent (pitch accent) language, not a stress language and, in the author's analysis, not a genuine tone language: one accent per word, realised as a single H tone (L = no accent), with downdrift/downstep operating on the surface tones. The accent is morphologically supplied (roots are neutral; the final obligatory suffix of nouns and infinitives, or verb markers/relators/pronouns, carry it) and is either fixed on that suffix syllable or floats one syllable to its left, so in nouns and infinitives it lands on the final or penultimate syllable; it is 'free' in the sense of not being tied to one fixed position, and residual root accents outrank morpheme accents when they compete. All-L and all-H polysyllabic nouns are explained as accent deletion under prefix+suffix derivation or /HBH/ plateauing. For a catalog record this reads as: culminative tonal accent, morphologically conditioned, final/penultimate; no dynamic (intensity) stress described. Supporting first-hand statements held by the project: Tchagbalé 1984 JWAL p. 30 (one H per phonological word, 'th' possibly an accent) and Müller 1905 §5 p. 253 (impressionistic dynamic accent within the last three syllables plus a H/L tone accent).

sources.quote: celui que, provisoirement, nous appelons th (ton haut) en attendant de voir s'il ne s'agit pas plutôt d'un accent. [...] Le symbole th est affecté du signe + si le lexème impose à un endroit quelconque du mot phonique un ton haut. Le mot phonique dont le lexème est + th ne porte qu'un ton haut. Le mot phonique qui se constitue autour du lexème -th sera à schème tonal monotone bas.
sources.note: Earlier statement of the same culminativity fact: each phonological word carries at most one H tone, treated as a lexeme-level prosodic feature 'th' that the author already suspects is an accent rather than a tone; no positional rule given here (position is fixed by the morphemes, see 2001). Consistent with and anticipates the 2001 tonal-accent analysis.

sources.quote: 2 tonèmes: H et B (haut et bas). Le ton H est représenté par un accent aigu, le ton B n'est pas marqué. [...] (Pour une analyse complète du système tonal en tem, voir Tchagbalé [1976].) [...] 1ère règle: Lorsqu'un ton B suit immédiatement un ton H, il est relevé au niveau de ce dernier, sauf en position finale de proposition. [...] 2ème règle: Lorsque deux tons H sont séparés par un ou plusieurs tons B à l'intérieur d'une même proposition, le deuxième est surbaissé par rapport au premier.
sources.locator: p. 2 (phoneme inventory) and §5 'La perturbation et les changements des tons', p. 31-32
sources.note: SIL description treating Tem as a two-tone (H/L) language with H-spreading and downstep rules and 'floating' tones in verb morphemes; no accent or stress statement. Silent on word stress; compatible with Tchagbalé 2001's surface facts.
